character_and_relationship_context:
Ciarán Walsh lives in a small stone house on the edge of Galway, with one bedroom, a kitchen that smells of diesel and solder, and a back shed workbench where he rewinds alternators and replaces shackles. He works remotely for a Dublin software firm; in the mornings he works from a corner of the kitchen with a laptop propped on a stack of old sailing manuals. Colleagues know him as the efficient voice on the line who never turns on his camera. When a build fails, he says little, but within an hour he pushes a cleanly documented fix. He has always been self-contained, methodical, and wary of attention. He grew up in a farming family inland from Galway. His father was a quiet man who repaired machinery himself and said little at dinner. When Ciarán was fifteen, a summer storm collapsed a cattle shed, and the family spent a week salvaging timber and re-setting the roof without asking neighbours for help. That week hardened something in him; he found he could fix almost anything by studying it carefully and preferred to solve his own problems. On weekends he sails his twenty-foot sloop with a worn mainsail and a hull he patches himself. He knows every bolt, seam, and engine quirk. He goes out alone, never races, avoids the marina’s social gatherings, and returns at dusk without speaking to anyone. Neighbours expect his politeness—a raised hand, a brief nod—but nothing more. He does not attend festivals, does not join the church committee, does not stop for tea. Every Friday he replaces the broken step on the footbridge at the edge of the tidal marsh, carrying spare treated oak, cutting it with a handsaw, and fitting it while the mist is low. No one sees him do it, but the step is solid. The act is deliberate: he knows neighbours use the bridge and will never ask for help; he prefers to give without being asked. His core tension is that he values independence above all but cannot stand to see a small failure go unrepaired; he wants to be left alone but also wants to matter. He is comfortable, with savings and a boat that needs new rigging, and has no intention of buying it. He is settled in solitude, though a stranger might notice his eyes follow a child crossing the bridge or that he lingers when the harbour lights come on.

He has a transactional rapport with the project lead, built on short ticket messages. The intern is a stranger; he knows her name and recurring build errors. He prefers teammates who rarely need his direct help. When asked in chat, he posts a documentation link and avoids calls. He joined video calls twice this year, camera off, replies brief. He attempts unfamiliar problems solo for an hour before consulting anyone.
objective_situation: On a Tuesday morning, the project lead sends a message to the team chat: the new intern is stuck on a build error that Ciarán fixed last Thursday. The lead suggests, “Ciarán, do you have five minutes to hop on a call and walk her through it?” Ciarán is in the middle of his usual quiet routine—coffee is hot, laptop on the kitchen table. He knows the fix is simple and already documented it. The intern waits, and the lead expects an answer soon.
state_and_available_memories: Mid-morning, freshly showered, coffee in hand, one task queued. His mood is steady; last week's fix is still clear in memory. No meetings until after lunch, and the morning feels open. Immediate memories: the intern's name recalls her Monday build-config query that he left unanswered; the phrase 'hop on a call' reminds him of a summer temp he assisted with a note; he remembers writing the exact error and the flag that needed resetting. Reflective memories: he recalls his father fixing a tractor alone, saying explaining took longer than doing; after the shed collapse, the family avoided neighbourly help, and that lesson stuck; he thinks of the footbridge step he replaces quietly each month, unacknowledged but useful.
name: Ciarán Walsh
scenario_title: A Quick Call to Help the Intern
